title: What is Structured Streaming — a scalable, fault-tolerant stream processing engine built on Spark SQL that treats a stream as an unbounded table and processes it incrementally in micro-batches — and how does it differ from the legacy DStream API (DataFrame/SQL API, Catalyst-optimized, exactly-once, event-time support)?
shortTitle: What is Structured Streaming and how it differs from DStreams

s1_definition.profdef: Structured Streaming is Spark's high-level stream processing engine built on the Spark SQL engine, which models a live stream as an unbounded input table that keeps growing as new data arrives, and runs your query incrementally so each micro-batch processes only the newly arrived rows while Spark maintains the result as if the whole table had been queried. Because it is expressed with the DataFrame and SQL API, it is optimized by Catalyst, supports event-time processing with watermarks, and provides end-to-end exactly-once guarantees through checkpointed offsets and idempotent sinks. It replaces the older DStream API, which was built on low-level RDDs, exposed a batch-of-RDDs model, had no built-in event-time or exactly-once support, and was not Catalyst-optimized.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India imagine a ledger that never closes — every new transaction is one more row appended to the bottom forever. Structured Streaming treats the live feed of transactions exactly like that endless ledger table, and every few seconds it processes just the new rows and keeps your running totals correct as if you had queried the whole ledger. The old DStream approach was like being handed a fresh stack of slips every second with no sense of when each transaction actually happened and no guarantee a slip was counted exactly once; the new engine gives you the familiar ledger (table) view, understands when each transaction truly occurred, and guarantees each is counted exactly once even after a crash.
s1_definition.oneliner: Structured Streaming treats a stream as an unbounded, ever-growing table processed incrementally with the Catalyst-optimized DataFrame API, event-time support, and exactly-once — unlike the low-level, batch-of-RDDs DStream API.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Structured Streaming is Spark's high-level stream processing engine built on the Spark SQL engine, which models a live stream as an unbounded input table that keeps growing as new data arrives, and runs your query incrementally so each micro-batch processes only the newly arrived rows while Spark maintains the result as if the whole table had been queried. Because it is expressed with the DataFrame and SQL API, it is optimized by Catalyst, supports event-time processing with watermarks, and provides end-to-end exactly-once guarantees through checkpointed offsets and idempotent sinks. It replaces the older DStream API, which was built on low-level RDDs, exposed a batch-of-RDDs model, had no built-in event-time or exactly-once support, and was not Catalyst-optimized.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India imagine a ledger that never closes — every new transaction is one more row appended to the bottom forever. Structured Streaming treats the live feed of transactions exactly like that endless ledger table, and every few seconds it processes just the new rows and keeps your running totals correct as if you had queried the whole ledger. The old DStream approach was like being handed a fresh stack of slips every second with no sense of when each transaction actually happened and no guarantee a slip was counted exactly once; the new engine gives you the familiar ledger (table) view, understands when each transaction truly occurred, and guarantees each is counted exactly once even after a crash.

**One line to remember:** Structured Streaming treats a stream as an unbounded, ever-growing table processed incrementally with the Catalyst-optimized DataFrame API, event-time support, and exactly-once — unlike the low-level, batch-of-RDDs DStream API.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is the unbounded table model. You write a normal DataFrame query — filters, aggregations, joins — against a streaming DataFrame, and Spark continuously updates the answer as new data arrives. You create the source with `spark.readStream.format("kafka").option(...).load()` and you start the query with `writeStream`. For example, counting transactions per account is simply `stream.groupBy("accountId").count()`, the exact same code you would write for a static DataFrame, and Spark turns it into an incremental streaming computation.

It runs as micro-batches by default. Spark periodically checks the source for new offsets, forms a small batch of the new rows, runs the incremental query, and writes the output, then repeats. This gives latency on the order of hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. There is also an experimental continuous mode for millisecond latency, but micro-batch is the production standard because it is robust and fully featured.

Because it is built on Spark SQL, every streaming query goes through the Catalyst Optimizer, so you get predicate pushdown, column pruning, and whole-stage code generation for free. This is a major advantage over DStreams, which operated on raw RDDs with no logical-plan optimization. You write high-level declarative code and Spark produces an efficient physical plan.

Event-time support and exactly-once are first-class. You can tell Spark which column holds the real event time and attach a watermark with `withWatermark("eventTime", "10 minutes")`, so late and out-of-order events are bucketed by when they actually happened rather than when Spark saw them. Combined with checkpointed offsets and idempotent or transactional sinks, Structured Streaming delivers end-to-end exactly-once results, which DStreams could only approximate at at-least-once.

A senior-level nuance is the mental model shift. In DStreams you thought in terms of a sequence of RDD batches and manually managed state and time. In Structured Streaming you think in terms of one logical query against an infinite table, and Spark manages incremental execution, state, watermarks, and recovery for you. This is why all new streaming work at a bank uses Structured Streaming, and DStreams are considered legacy.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants a live count of transactions per account from a Kafka feed. The team should write the same DataFrame code they already know, not a special low-level streaming API. This is exactly the unbounded-table model where a `groupBy("accountId").count()` runs incrementally.

Problem 2 — Transactions sometimes arrive late or out of order because of network delays. The count must reflect when the transaction actually happened, not when Spark received it. This is event-time with a watermark, which DStreams did not support.

Problem 3 — If the job crashes mid-stream, each transaction must still be counted exactly once on restart. This is checkpointing plus idempotent sinks giving exactly-once, which DStreams could not guarantee.

Because a real Kafka cluster is not available in this runnable demo, the code simulates the unbounded-table concept with an in-memory stream of transaction events and an incremental per-account counter, logging how each micro-batch updates the running result, while the explanation maps each simulated step to the real Structured Streaming API call it represents.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two micro-batches of transaction events. Batch 1 has two for SAV2001 and one for CUR3001. Batch 2 has one more each for SAV2001 and CUR3001.

Step 1: Batch 1 arrives, standing in for `readStream` pulling new Kafka offsets. The incremental counter merges each row into the running map. SAV2001 becomes 2 and CUR3001 becomes 1. The result table is a snapshot of these counts.

Step 2: The demo logs the result table after batch 1, representing what the streaming sink would emit for this trigger.

Step 3: Batch 2 arrives as the next trigger. The same query runs incrementally — Spark does not reprocess batch 1, it only adds the new rows. SAV2001 becomes 3 and CUR3001 becomes 2.

Step 4: The result table after batch 2 is logged. In real Structured Streaming this state would be checkpointed so a crash-and-restart would resume exactly here, giving exactly-once counts.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 05:02:10 INFO    Micro-batch 1 arrives (readStream → incremental query)
2026-10-30 05:02:10 INFO    Result table after batch 1: {SAV2001=2, CUR3001=1}
2026-10-30 05:02:10 INFO    Micro-batch 2 arrives (same query runs incrementally)
2026-10-30 05:02:10 INFO    Result table after batch 2: {SAV2001=3, CUR3001=2}
2026-10-30 05:02:10 INFO    Structured Streaming unbounded-table simulation complete.
```

```

    │  new offsets per trigger

  readStream.format("kafka").load()  → streaming DataFrame (unbounded table)
    │
    ▼
  groupBy("accountId").count()  → incremental query (Catalyst-optimized)
    │
    ├─ micro-batch 1: {SAV2001=2, CUR3001=1}

  writeStream.outputMode("update") → sink

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Structured Streaming is Spark's modern stream processing engine, and the single most important idea is that it treats a live stream as an unbounded table that keeps growing as new data arrives. You write an ordinary DataFrame or SQL query against that table, and Spark runs it incrementally, processing only the newly arrived rows in each micro-batch while maintaining the result as if you had queried the entire table. Because it is built on the Spark SQL engine, every streaming query is optimized by Catalyst with predicate pushdown, column pruning, and code generation, so you get a high-level declarative API and an efficient physical plan at the same time.

It differs from the legacy DStream API in several decisive ways. DStreams were built on low-level RDDs and exposed a sequence-of-batches model where you manually managed time and state, had no real event-time support, were not Catalyst-optimized, and could only reach at-least-once delivery. Structured Streaming gives you the familiar DataFrame API, first-class event-time processing with watermarks so late and out-of-order data is bucketed by when it actually happened, and end-to-end exactly-once results through checkpointed offsets combined with idempotent or transactional sinks.

At the National Bank of India I used this to maintain a live per-account transaction count from a Kafka feed. The code was literally a groupBy on account id with a count, the same expression I would write for a static table, and Spark turned it into an incremental streaming computation that updated every few seconds. Late transactions were handled correctly by attaching a watermark on the event-time column, and the checkpoint location let the job restart after a crash and resume with exactly-once counts. In interviews I summarize it as: one logical query against an infinite table, run incrementally, with Catalyst optimization, event-time correctness, and exactly-once — everything the old DStream API lacked.

---

keyPoints: Structured Streaming: micro-batch or continuous processing
Watermark: handle late data — discard after threshold
Checkpoint: fault tolerance — recover state on failure
